passage:
Bidisha's first pay had gone straight to her parents. Every month since, she sent part of her salary to Kolkata, and lent to friends who asked. By the fourth month she was checking her bank app before buying lunch, and she had started to dread Shalini's calls.
On Sunday, Shalini rang again. "Just until the month end, Bidi."
Bidisha looked at her notebook, where she had finally listed what she needed for rent, food, and one small saving. She breathed. "Shalini, I can lend you a little this once. After that I can't keep lending. I have to keep some for myself."
There was silence. "I didn't realise it was hard for you," Shalini said, quieter. "Okay. I'll ask my cousin for the rest."
Bidisha put the phone down. She felt lighter, and a little sad.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha send part of her salary every month?
qa.a: She sent part of it to her parents in Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling in the weeks before she spoke to Shalini?
qa.a: She was anxious and resentful. She checked her bank app before buying lunch and dreaded Shalini's calls.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that made her giving more sustainable?
qa.a: She wrote down what she needed for rent, food and saving. She lent a little once and said clearly that she could not keep lending.

qa.q: How did Shalini seem to take Bidisha's limit?
qa.a: Shalini went quiet, then said she had not realised it was hard for Bidisha and would ask a cousin. This suggests Shalini was surprised but accepted it.

grounding: A young earner supports others but sets a limit so giving does not turn into resentment.

passage:
Mohit's younger sister Payal leaned on the kitchen counter. "Bhaiya, my college needs the whole fee for the trip by Friday. Can you pay it? You earn now."
Mohit stirred his tea. "How much is it?"
"It's a lot. But everyone's going."
"I'll pay half."
"Half? That's not enough!"
"It's what I can give without going short on what I send Mummy every month, and my own bills. I want to help you, Payal, not lose track of me."
She crossed her arms. "You sound like Papa."
"Maybe. Ask the college about instalments. And you could keep your tuition money for part of the rest?"
Payal sighed. "Fine. Half is better than nothing."
"Thank you for not shouting," said Mohit. "I do want you to go."

qa.q: How much of the trip fee did Mohit say he would pay?
qa.a: He said he would pay half.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling as he named his limit?
qa.a: Mohit felt caring but firm, and a little worried about hurting Payal. His wish to help, his thanks for not shouting and his line that he wants her to go all show it.

qa.q: What could Mohit and Payal do next so that the trip fee is still covered?
qa.a: Payal could ask the college about paying in instalments and use part of her own tuition money, as Mohit suggested.

qa.q: How might Payal feel about Mohit offering only half?
qa.a: Payal felt disappointed and annoyed at first, as her crossed arms and the remark that he sounded like Papa show, though she then accepted half as better than nothing.

grounding: A young earner helps a younger sister but names a sustainable limit so that giving does not turn into resentment.

passage:
When my first nursing salary came in, I felt rich for about two days. Then the messages started. Appa's roof repair. My cousin Manjula's college fees. A friend's birthday trip. Amma's "small thing" that wasn't small.
I said yes to everything for four months. By the fifth, I was eating instant noodles at night and snapping at Manjula on the phone for no reason. I hated who I was becoming.
So I sat with Appa and was honest. I told him how much I could send home each month without going under, and that I'd help Manjula with fees but not the new phone she wanted. He was quiet, then said, "You're right, Sudha. We forget you have a life too."
I still give. I just don't resent it anymore.

qa.q: Whose college fees did the narrator help with?
qa.a: Manjula's college fees.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling by the fifth month?
qa.a: Sudha felt worn out and resentful, snapping at Manjula for no reason and disliking the person Sudha was becoming.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Sudha's position?
qa.a: Have an honest talk with family about what can be given without going under, and, if money worries grow, talk it through with a trusted adult or qualified adviser.

qa.q: How did Appa respond to Sudha's honesty?
qa.a: Appa was quiet, then admitted the family forgets Sudha has a life too, which suggests he felt a little guilty and understood.

grounding: Shows a young earner who supports family and a cousin but sets a sustainable limit so that giving stops turning into resentment.

passage:
Team lead's note, customer support, Hyderabad, end of quarter.
Dhruv has been in the team eight months and is the first to say yes to anything. He covers colleagues' night shifts, stays late to fix others' tickets, and I've seen him lend money to two people this month. Last week he was short with a customer for the first time, and Kalyani told me he'd skipped lunch four days running.
I asked him to coffee. He said, "If I say no, people will think I don't care." I asked what he could keep giving for a year without breaking. He thought hard and said: one extra shift a month, and help with tickets before six.
He told the team on Monday. Kalyani took over the extra nights. Today he laughed on a call, the first time in weeks. I'll check in with him again next month.

qa.q: How long has Dhruv been in the team?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about if he said no?
qa.a: He was anxious that people would think he didn't care about them.

qa.q: What small step did the team lead suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: They asked what Dhruv could keep giving for a year without breaking, which let him set his own limit instead of stopping giving altogether.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see the change?
qa.a: Kalyani had noticed him skipping lunch, so she is probably relieved and glad to share the extra nights.

grounding: Shows a young earner who gives time and help to everyone learning to set a limit so his generosity can last.

passage:
Friday, late.
Deepak called again. My younger brother needs his bike fixed, needs a new phone cover, needs "just a little" for a trip with his friends. Last month I paid his college exam fee, and I was proud to.
Tonight I said yes to the exam fee part of next term and no to the trip. My voice shook. He went silent, then said "fine" and hung up.
I sat on my bed and felt like the worst person in the family. Then I looked at my own list. Rent. My course. The dentist I've been putting off for a year.
If I keep saying yes to everything, one day I'll say no to everything, angrily. I'd rather say a small no now.
Still feel guilty. Also, strangely, lighter.
Suraj

qa.q: What did Suraj pay for last month?
qa.a: Suraj paid Deepak's college exam fee.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after Deepak hung up?
qa.a: Suraj felt guilty, like the worst person in the family, and also strangely lighter.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next time Deepak asks?
qa.a: Suraj could explain calmly what help is possible and why, so Deepak understands the limit is about lasting, not about not caring.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when he heard no to the trip?
qa.a: Deepak was probably disappointed and a little hurt, going silent before saying 'fine' and hanging up.

grounding: Shows a young earner who keeps supporting a sibling's important needs but says no to extras so giving does not turn into resentment.

passage:
Joseph read the message twice before he answered.
Siddharth: bro, one more favour. Can you lend me something for a new phone? Mine's cracked
Joseph: Sid, I can't this month.
Siddharth: Come on, you just got your increment 😅
Joseph: I did. A big part goes home for Chechi's college fees, and I've kept aside what I need to get through the month.
Siddharth: So you're saying no.
Joseph: I'm saying no to money. Not to you. I'll come on Saturday and help you fix your CV for the bank job, and I know a repair shop that can change the screen.
Siddharth: ...ok fine. Sorry, I've asked a lot lately.
Joseph: You have 🙂 But I'd rather say no now than start avoiding your calls.
Siddharth: Fair. Saturday, 5?
Joseph: Saturday, 5. Bring the phone.

qa.q: What will Joseph help Siddharth with on Saturday?
qa.a: He will help Siddharth fix his CV for the bank job, and Siddharth is to bring the phone.

qa.q: What does Joseph's line about avoiding calls suggest he is worried about?
qa.a: He is worried that giving past his limit would turn into resentment and make him avoid his friend, which he fears more than saying no.

qa.q: What worked in the way Joseph said no?
qa.a: He was clear about the limit, gave a short reason without over-explaining, and offered help he could truly give, like the CV and the repair shop.

qa.q: How did Siddharth take the refusal?
qa.a: He pushed a little at first, then apologised for asking a lot and fixed a time, so the friendship stayed intact.

grounding: Shows a young earner who supports his family setting a clear limit with a friend so that giving does not turn into resentment.
